newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: BOTSWANA TELECOM YEAR PROFITS HALVED AS COSTS BITE.
newsitem.headline: BOTSWANA TELECOM YEAR PROFITS HALVED AS COSTS BITE.

text.p: Botswana Telecommunications Corp (BTC), a possible candidate for privatisation, saw its after-tax profit more than halved to 8.4 million pula from 18.5 million in the year ended March 31.
BTC said the earnings slump was despite a jump in turnover to 200.7 million pula from 185.1 million a year ago.
The bottom line was hit by an increase of 22.5 million pula to 155.1 million in operating costs and, due in part to the depreciation in the pula. Finance costs rose 3.3 million to 37.3 million.
The majority of the increase in operating expenses reflected a 13 percent increase in staff costs and higher depreciation charges.

"The pula (which is indirectly linked to the South African rand) has depreciated against all major currencies. As our loans and expenses are serviced in foreign currencies, this had a serious impact on our profitability," chairman A.V. Lionjanga said in the company's annual report.
Foreign loans stood at 40.8 million rand at the end of the year.

During the year, BTC spent 49 million rand on transmission and telephone equipment increasing the book value of its equipment by 12 percent to 620 million percent. Depreciation under these headings was 56 million.
Parliament earlier this year amended the Botswana Telecommunications Act to open up the industry to competition
and set up a Telecommunications Authority which will regulate tariffs and issue licences.
BTC chief executive, Olebile Gaborone, told reporters that BTC had found a joint venture partner, the Global One alliance, to introduce Internet services to Botswana.
It was also negotiating with other companies to bring in a cellular telephone service.
During the coming year, BTC will proceed with a telephone link between Botswana and Namibia at a cost of 19 million pula.
Botswana's private sector last month listed parastatals it considered ripe for privatisation -- including BTC -- in a report welcomed by the government.
